title: Tumour board decision template: long inputs near the context budget, a superseded first decision and a refused acceptance of it
notes: Expert path: a multi-site design with dependency closure, long inputs and two decisions where the second withdraws the first. Inputs are long by design: a 605-word need (3711 characters), 1328 characters of constraints and 12 local facts of up to 400 characters each (4001 characters). By the generator's estimate, carrying them whole with the nine abstracts gives a Scan appraisal context of about 18,700 characters, and carrying every field the 875fe59 view selects unclipped as well gives a largest context (the manuscript call) of about 31,700 characters, 99 percent of MAX_COMPACT_CHARS (32,000). No call may be refused for size; anything cut to fit must be a model-written field named as cut, never the investigator's text or a source abstract (S4, D6, stated in step notes, not asserted); the stored need, constraints and export stay exactly as typed. Routing is pragmatic-trial (explicit under both classifier rules). The problem reply condenses the constraints: G11 keeps the typed text and records rejected-change (counted under S11, the closest listed entry), a refusal the scenario states. The appraisal of nine records (one undated, kept null) records six claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. The first design reply proposes a parallel cluster comparison (recommended 'rct', gate unknown): the proposal must not change study.family (S11 with D3). The investigator drafts Protocol and Analysis on it; the analysis shows about 40 percent power. The revised design reply proposes a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial on the six-wave schedule and supersedes the first decision (withdrawn, kept), flagging Protocol and Analysis for review (G8). An attempt to accept the withdrawn first decision is refused (A1 item A2), then the second is accepted (accepted, ready, basis explicit); redoing Protocol and Analysis clears the flags. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (ev-0uwsqis, ev-1apyzii, ev-0veejcb, ev-06uylmy, ev-17kagtg, ev-0ul2jhz) and titleYearKey hash for records 2, 8, 9 (ev-1ktt1wv, ev-0mqhpb3, ev-1raixmt). Requires S11, S13 and D5. Catches: clipped or replaced investigator input, a proposal that sets the family, a superseded decision erased or accepted, and stale downstream stages counted complete.

inputs.need:
I am a medical oncologist and chair the tumour board working group of a regional cancer network of six hospitals. Between them the hospitals run 11 multidisciplinary tumour boards (breast, lung, colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, urology, gynaecology, head and neck, skin, haematology, brain and spine, and sarcoma) that discuss about 18,000 cases a year. Each board's decisions are typed into the board software as free text by whoever is minuting that week, and the quality of that text varies enormously from board to board and from week to week.

Last year our working group reviewed 600 randomly sampled case discussions against seven items that any clinician picking up the case should be able to find: the stage used for the decision, performance status, the treatment recommended, the reason when the recommendation departs from the network guideline, whether trial eligibility was considered, the patient's known preferences, and who will tell the patient and by when. Only 54 percent of discussions documented all seven. The weakest items were the patient's preferences (documented in 31 percent) and the reason for departing from the guideline (41 percent). We found cases where the treating team could not tell from the minutes what had been agreed, two complaints from patients who were told different plans by different clinicians, and a clear pattern of longer waits from board to first treatment when the minutes were incomplete.

The network has agreed to introduce a structured decision template built into the board software, together with a trained board coordinator at each hospital and a short monthly feedback report to each board chair. Because of software licensing and coordinator recruitment, the template cannot go live everywhere at once, and the network's digital team proposes to switch boards on in six waves between February and December 2027. Every board will have the template by the end of 2027, and nobody is willing to hold a board back beyond that.

I would like to use this rollout to run a pragmatic trial that answers two questions: does the template package increase the proportion of case discussions with complete decision documentation, and does it shorten the time from board discussion to first treatment without making meetings longer or reducing the number of cases each board can discuss? I am not sure how to allocate boards to waves, whether 11 boards are enough to answer the question, how to handle boards of very different sizes (the breast board discusses about 60 cases a week, the sarcoma board about 8), or whether the unit of analysis should be the board, the meeting or the case discussion.

There are practical limits. Our data manager can extract the minutes and treatment dates, but only three days a month. The template can be switched on per board but not per case. Board chairs will know when their board has the template, and so will the coordinators who complete it, so nobody can be blinded. Two hospitals are merging their information systems in the middle of 2027, which may disrupt data extraction for their four boards for about two months. Patient representatives on the network board have asked that patients' own understanding of their treatment plan is measured, not just the paperwork, and board chairs have asked that nothing we add takes more than ten minutes of meeting time.

I need help turning this into a design the network board can approve in November: the allocation, the outcome definitions, the sample size reasoning, the analysis, the ethics route for using minutes and treatment dates without individual consent, and what to measure so that we notice if the template simply produces longer minutes that nobody reads.
inputs.constraints: The template goes live in six waves between February and December 2027 and every board must have it by the end of 2027; no board can be held back longer than that. The data manager has three days a month for extraction of minutes and treatment dates, and there is no research budget beyond the coordinator salaries the network already funds. The template is switched on per board, never per case, and nobody can be blinded to it. Two hospitals merge their information systems in mid-2027, which may interrupt extraction for their four boards for about two months. Any patient-reported measure must take no more than five minutes and be available in the network's four most common languages. Board chairs have asked that the evaluation adds no more than ten minutes to any meeting and that individual clinicians are never named in feedback or reports. The network board meets in November 2026 to approve the design, and a design that needs individual patient consent to use minutes and treatment dates is not workable at this scale. Results go to the network board for each hospital without ranking boards against each other, and the patient representatives must see the questionnaire and its translations before any patient receives it. Any change to the wave dates needs the digital team's agreement at least eight weeks ahead.
localFacts: The network's six hospitals run 11 tumour boards that discussed 17,940 cases between September 2025 and August 2026; the breast board discussed 3,050 and the sarcoma board 410, and the median board about 1,500 over that year. Board lists range from about 8 cases a week (sarcoma) to about 60 (breast), and the three largest boards meet at the two teaching hospitals.

The working group's 2025 review of 600 randomly sampled case discussions found all seven decision items documented in 54 percent; patient preferences were documented in 31 percent and the reason for departing from the guideline in 41 percent (working group report WG-TB-2025-04). Two reviewers from outside each board agreed on 92 percent of items in a double-reviewed subsample.

In the same review, the median time from board discussion to first treatment was 19 days when all seven items were documented and 26 days when any item was missing; the difference was not adjusted for case mix. Discussions with a missing item were also more often repeated within a month (14 percent against 6 percent).

The network board approved the template package and a six-wave rollout between February and December 2027 on 2026-06-11 (minute NB-2026-06-11); the order in which boards join the waves was left to the working group. The waves start in February, April, June, August, October and December, each at the first meeting of the month.

The research ethics board approved an evaluation of the rollout in which every board receives the template during 2027, using minutes and treatment dates without individual consent (approval REB-CN-2026-118, dated 2026-08-29); any design that withholds the template into 2028 is not covered. Patient questionnaires need verbal or online consent.

The digital team can switch on at most two boards per wave because of software licensing and training capacity; boards cannot be switched on for some cases and not others, and the software has no allocation feature. Each switch-on takes a half-day configuration session and one training meeting with the board's coordinator and chair.

The data manager can extract minutes and treatment dates for three days a month, which the working group estimates at about 220 case discussions a month if each takes about five minutes to review against the seven items. Minutes come from the board software and treatment dates from the hospital systems.

Hospitals D and E merge their information systems between June and August 2027; their four boards (colorectal, urology, skin and head and neck) may have no extractable minutes or treatment dates for about two months. The merger date has already moved twice, and the information teams will confirm it in March 2027.

Board coordinators are funded at every hospital from January 2027 under network budget line CN-2027-COORD, and each coordinator will complete two days of training on the template before their board's wave starts. Four of the six coordinators are new posts; two hospitals are moving existing administrative staff into the role.

The network's patient representatives asked on 2026-05-20 that patients' understanding of their treatment plan be measured with a short questionnaire, offered in the four most common languages, rather than inferred from the minutes. The four languages are English, Polish, Urdu and Portuguese, and the patient experience team can fund translation.

Board chairs agreed on 2026-07-02 to receive a monthly one-page feedback report on their own board's documentation, provided that no individual clinician is named and that no report is shared outside the board. Two chairs asked that the report compare their board with its own previous months rather than with other boards.

The board software records the start and end time of each meeting and the number of cases discussed, which allows meeting duration and cases per meeting to be measured for every board from January 2026 onward. Meetings currently last a median of 95 minutes, and the longest board regularly overruns its two-hour slot.

response.subtitle: Pragmatic trial using the network's six-wave rollout of a structured decision template
response.statement: Across 11 tumour boards in six hospitals, only 54 percent of sampled case discussions documented all seven core decision items, with patient preferences recorded in 31 percent and the reason for departing from the guideline in 41 percent. Incomplete minutes are linked to longer waits for first treatment and to patients hearing different plans. A structured template with board coordinators and monthly feedback will reach every board in six waves during 2027, and the network needs a pragmatic trial within that rollout to show whether documentation improves and treatment starts sooner without longer meetings.

records.title: Structured templates for multidisciplinary team decisions: effect on documentation completeness in a cancer centre
records.authors: Halloran-Mensah D, Richter-Oyelaran S, Nakamura-Blake P
records.abstract: We introduced a structured decision template in the multidisciplinary meetings of one cancer centre and compared 400 case discussions before with 400 after. The proportion of discussions documenting all core decision items rose from 48 to 81 percent. The largest gains were in the reason for departing from guidelines and the named person who would inform the patient. Meeting length did not change. The comparison was uncontrolled, and the template was introduced alongside a new meeting chair. Staff reported that the template made the recommendation easier to find in the record.

records.title: Quality of multidisciplinary tumour board decision records: a multicentre review of 2,400 case discussions
records.abstract: We reviewed 2,400 case discussions from 16 tumour boards in eight hospitals against a list of core decision items. Only 52 percent of discussions documented every item, and patient preferences were documented in 29 percent. Completeness varied more between boards than between hospitals, and boards with a dedicated coordinator had higher completeness. Minutes written during the meeting were more complete than minutes written afterwards. The review did not examine consequences for patients. Boards that recorded decisions directly into the electronic record were no more complete than boards using paper forms.

records.title: Board coordinators and decision recording in cancer multidisciplinary meetings: a stepped rollout across nine hospitals
records.authors: Okwuosa-Brandt F, Carlsson-Mbeki J, Ferreira-Holt E
records.abstract: Nine hospitals introduced trained board coordinators in a stepped sequence over 12 months, and we compared documentation completeness before and after each hospital's start date, adjusting for calendar time. Completeness rose by 22 percentage points after coordinators started. The intraclass correlation for completeness within boards was 0.12. The order of hospitals was set by recruitment, not by chance, and two hospitals changed their board software during the study. Coordinators spent most of their added time preparing case lists and chasing missing items before each meeting.

records.title: Incomplete tumour board documentation and time to first treatment: a linked records analysis
records.abstract: We linked 3,180 tumour board discussions to treatment records in one region. After adjustment for tumour site, stage and age, discussions with incomplete decision documentation were followed by first treatment a median of 7 days later than discussions with complete documentation. Incomplete documentation was also associated with more repeat discussions of the same patient. Residual confounding by case complexity is likely, because complex cases are both harder to document and slower to treat. The analysis could not separate the effect of documentation from the effect of the board's workload.

records.title: Patient understanding of treatment plans after multidisciplinary discussion: development and validation of a five-item questionnaire
records.abstract: We developed a five-item questionnaire asking patients whether they know their planned treatment, its purpose, the next step, who to contact and whether their preferences were discussed. In 612 patients it took a median of 4 minutes to complete, showed good test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation 0.84) and distinguished patients whose clinicians rated communication as poor. Versions in three languages other than English were tested with 140 patients. Patients with limited literacy needed help to complete it. Scores were not related to the patient's age or tumour site.

records.title: Meeting duration and case throughput after introducing structured decision templates in tumour boards
records.abstract: We measured meeting duration and cases discussed per meeting in seven tumour boards for six months before and after they adopted a structured decision template. Meetings were a mean of 6 minutes longer in the first month after adoption and returned to their previous length by the third month. The number of cases discussed per meeting did not change. Boards whose coordinators prepared the template before the meeting saw the smallest increase in duration. No board reported dropping cases from the agenda to make room for the template.

records.title: Stepped-wedge cluster trials with few clusters: power, secular trends and analysis choices
records.abstract: We examined the power and bias of stepped-wedge and parallel cluster designs with between 8 and 16 clusters using simulation. With 12 clusters and an intraclass correlation of 0.10 or more, a stepped-wedge design reached 80 percent power where a parallel cluster design with the same clusters reached 41 percent. Stepped-wedge designs were sensitive to secular trends, which had to be modelled explicitly, and to disruptions in data collection affecting some clusters. Randomising the order of clusters within strata of cluster size reduced imbalance.

records.title: Feedback reports to tumour board chairs and sustained documentation quality
records.abstract: After a documentation template was introduced in five tumour boards, three boards received monthly feedback reports on completeness and two did not. Completeness was similar at three months, but at 12 months it remained above 80 percent in boards receiving feedback and had fallen to 63 percent in the others. Chairs valued reports that compared their board with its own past performance rather than with other boards. Allocation to feedback was by chair preference. The authors call for a randomised comparison of feedback strategies.

records.title: Recording multidisciplinary team decisions: a minimum dataset for cancer services
records.abstract: The committee sets out a minimum dataset for recording multidisciplinary cancer team decisions: the stage and performance status used, the recommendation and its rationale, deviation from guidelines with reasons, trial eligibility, patient preferences and the person responsible for informing the patient. It recommends recording the decision during the meeting and auditing completeness regularly. The document gives no publication date and describes its development process only briefly. It asks services to report completeness for each team annually and to act on items that are often missing.

response.synthesis: Nine retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Before-after and stepped studies suggest that structured templates and coordinators raise documentation completeness by roughly 20 to 30 percentage points, with a within-board intraclass correlation of about 0.12, and that monthly feedback sustains the gain. Incomplete documentation is linked to later first treatment, though confounded by case complexity. Meetings lengthen briefly after adoption. A validated five-item questionnaire measures patients' understanding in about 4 minutes. Methods work shows that with about a dozen clusters a stepped-wedge design has far more power than a parallel cluster design, provided secular trends are modelled.
response.gradeRationale: No randomised evaluation of templates; consistent before-after and stepped observational evidence at risk of bias; methods and measurement evidence is stronger but indirect.

response.rationale: The analysis stage showed that a parallel comparison of 11 boards has about 40 percent power, and licensing allows only two boards per wave. The network's six-wave schedule is itself the better design: a pragmatic stepped-wedge cluster trial in which the order of boards is set by chance within strata of board size, so every board contributes before and after periods and every board has the template by December 2027. Planning values come from claims c1 and c4; time to first treatment (claim c3) and meeting duration (claim c5) are secondary and balancing outcomes. Secular trends are modelled, and the four boards affected by the information system merger are placed in waves away from June to August 2027. Reporting follows the CONSORT extension for stepped-wedge cluster trials.

response.designSummary: Stepped-wedge cluster design: 11 boards, seven monthly-grouped periods (baseline and six waves), repeated cross-sections of sampled discussions.
response.sampleSize: Each board contributes 20 sampled discussions a month for 12 months (about 2,640 discussions). Using the standard closed-form power approximation for stepped-wedge designs with an intraclass correlation of 0.12 (claim c2) and a cluster autocorrelation of 0.8, the design has about 85 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a rise in completeness from 54 to 74 percent, against about 40 percent for a parallel comparison of the same boards (claim c4). A simulation with the actual wave schedule and the two-month data gap for four boards will confirm this before the network board meets.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of completeness on the intervention indicator with fixed period effects and a random board intercept, adjusted for board size stratum; the treatment effect reported as an odds ratio and a risk difference with 95 percent intervals, and small-sample corrected standard errors because there are only 11 boards.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Linear mixed model for log time to first treatment with the same structure; understanding score by exposure; meeting duration and cases per meeting by exposure and months since switch-on; sensitivity analyses excluding the four merging boards' affected months and allowing the effect to vary with time since switch-on.
response.missingData: Months without extractable data for the merging boards are treated as missing at random given board and period, with a sensitivity analysis under a pattern-mixture assumption; questionnaire non-response is reported by language.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary and balancing outcomes are reported with intervals and without formal adjustment.
response.software: R (glmmTMB) with a documented simulation script archived before the first wave.
overfittingGuards: Period effects and adjustment fixed in advance
No board-level subgroup analyses beyond size strata
Analysis plan registered before the first wave
response.summary: About 85 percent power with 11 boards on the six-wave schedule; period effects modelled; small-sample corrections.

response.data: Extracts are pseudonymised by the data manager; board and hospital identifiers are kept for the analysis; no clinician is named in any report; feedback reports go only to the board chair.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with limited English or literacy, older patients and those from deprived areas are most at risk of mixed messages and least likely to complete questionnaires. response.effectiveness: The trial shows whether the package improves documentation and patient-facing outcomes during a rollout that is happening anyway.
response.efficiency: Uses the rollout, existing coordinators and three data-manager days a month.
response.costs: No research budget beyond coordinator salaries already funded; questionnaire printing and translation from the network's patient experience budget.
response.grants: None needed for the trial; results may support a national case for coordinator posts.
response.partnerships: Board chairs, coordinators, the digital team, the patient representatives and the two merging hospitals' information teams.
response.rebPath: Approved by the research ethics board (REB-CN-2026-118) for an evaluation in which every board receives the template in 2027; the stepped-wedge design is within that approval, while the superseded parallel design with a December start was also within it but underpowered.

response.summary: Waiver for routine data, consented questionnaire, equity reporting by language and age.

store.title: A structured decision template for tumour boards: a pragmatic trial across a six-hospital cancer network
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am a medical oncologist and chair the tumour board working group of a regional cancer network of six hospitals. Between them the hospitals run 11 multidisciplinary tumour boards (breast, lung, colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, urology, gynaecology, head and neck, skin, haematology, brain and spine, and sarcoma) that discuss about 18,000 cases a year. Each board's decisions are typed into the board software as free text by whoever is minuting that week, and the quality of that text varies enormously from board to board and from week to week.

Last year our working group reviewed 600 randomly sampled case discussions against seven items that any clinician picking up the case should be able to find: the stage used for the decision, performance status, the treatment recommended, the reason when the recommendation departs from the network guideline, whether trial eligibility was considered, the patient's known preferences, and who will tell the patient and by when. Only 54 percent of discussions documented all seven. The weakest items were the patient's preferences (documented in 31 percent) and the reason for departing from the guideline (41 percent). We found cases where the treating team could not tell from the minutes what had been agreed, two complaints from patients who were told different plans by different clinicians, and a clear pattern of longer waits from board to first treatment when the minutes were incomplete.

The network has agreed to introduce a structured decision template built into the board software, together with a trained board coordinator at each hospital and a short monthly feedback report to each board chair. Because of software licensing and coordinator recruitment, the template cannot go live everywhere at once, and the network's digital team proposes to switch boards on in six waves between February and December 2027. Every board will have the template by the end of 2027, and nobody is willing to hold a board back beyond that.

I would like to use this rollout to run a pragmatic trial that answers two questions: does the template package increase the proportion of case discussions with complete decision documentation, and does it shorten the time from board discussion to first treatment without making meetings longer or reducing the number of cases each board can discuss? I am not sure how to allocate boards to waves, whether 11 boards are enough to answer the question, how to handle boards of very different sizes (the breast board discusses about 60 cases a week, the sarcoma board about 8), or whether the unit of analysis should be the board, the meeting or the case discussion.

There are practical limits. Our data manager can extract the minutes and treatment dates, but only three days a month. The template can be switched on per board but not per case. Board chairs will know when their board has the template, and so will the coordinators who complete it, so nobody can be blinded. Two hospitals are merging their information systems in the middle of 2027, which may disrupt data extraction for their four boards for about two months. Patient representatives on the network board have asked that patients' own understanding of their treatment plan is measured, not just the paperwork, and board chairs have asked that nothing we add takes more than ten minutes of meeting time.

I need help turning this into a design the network board can approve in November: the allocation, the outcome definitions, the sample size reasoning, the analysis, the ethics route for using minutes and treatment dates without individual consent, and what to measure so that we notice if the template simply produces longer minutes that nobody reads.
store.problem.constraints: The template goes live in six waves between February and December 2027 and every board must have it by the end of 2027; no board can be held back longer than that. The data manager has three days a month for extraction of minutes and treatment dates, and there is no research budget beyond the coordinator salaries the network already funds. The template is switched on per board, never per case, and nobody can be blinded to it. Two hospitals merge their information systems in mid-2027, which may interrupt extraction for their four boards for about two months. Any patient-reported measure must take no more than five minutes and be available in the network's four most common languages. Board chairs have asked that the evaluation adds no more than ten minutes to any meeting and that individual clinicians are never named in feedback or reports. The network board meets in November 2026 to approve the design, and a design that needs individual patient consent to use minutes and treatment dates is not workable at this scale. Results go to the network board for each hospital without ranking boards against each other, and the patient representatives must see the questionnaire and its translations before any patient receives it. Any change to the wave dates needs the digital team's agreement at least eight weeks ahead.

response.title: A structured decision template package for tumour boards: a pragmatic stepped-wedge cluster trial across a regional cancer network
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether a structured decision template with board coordinators and monthly feedback increases complete documentation of tumour board decisions, shortens time to first treatment and improves patients' understanding without lengthening meetings. Design: pragmatic stepped-wedge cluster trial across 11 boards in six hospitals, with the order of boards set by chance within size strata on the network's six-wave rollout in 2027. Results and conclusions will follow the trial.
response.introduction: Only about half of sampled tumour board discussions document every core decision item, and incomplete documentation is linked to delays and conflicting messages to patients. Structured templates and coordinators have been evaluated only in before-after or convenience-ordered studies.
response.methods: Twenty discussions per board per month are reviewed against seven items by reviewers from other hospitals; treatment dates and meeting times come from routine systems; patients complete a five-item understanding questionnaire. Analysis uses mixed-effects models with period effects and small-sample corrections. A parallel design first considered was superseded because it was underpowered and incompatible with the licensing schedule.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present completeness by period and exposure, time to first treatment, understanding scores, meeting duration and delivery measures.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the effect against secular trends, the data gap for four boards and the few clusters, and state what the network should keep.
response.limitations: Eleven clusters; unblinded delivery; possible secular trends; a two-month data gap for four boards.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial; it will not claim effects on survival.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for stepped-wedge cluster randomised trials, with TIDieR
response.summary: CONSORT-structured draft with results left empty.
